chief_complaint: newborn infant with failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours, abdominal distension, and salty skin sweat
hpi_details: 3-week-old male presenting with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, foul-smelling oily stools, and history of meconium ileus at birth where quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis Sweat Chloride test confirms elevated chloride >60 mmol/L and delta F508 CFTR mutation.
ideas: She thinks her baby has a severe milk allergy or that her breast milk lacks nutrients because his stools are greasy and he is not gaining weight.
concerns: She is terrified that her baby is starving and will suffer permanent growth delays or brain damage if he cannot absorb nutrients.
expectations: She hopes to receive a prescription for a specialized hypoallergenic formula or digestive drops to help him start gaining weight.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Cystic fibrosis with meconium ileus and failure to thrive evaluation and management
core_concepts: Meconium ileus plus a sweat chloride concentration greater than 60 mmol/L and two CF-causing CFTR variants supports cystic fibrosis in this infant.
At 3 weeks, failure to thrive and steatorrhea suggest pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and require prompt nutrition and CF-center assessment.
First establish stability: obtain weight, temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, hydration status, abdominal examination, and urine output.
Bilious vomiting, worsening distension, lethargy, fever, dehydration, or reduced urine output may indicate obstruction, sepsis, or electrolyte disturbance and need emergency assessment.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: newborn infant with failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours, abdominal distension, and salty skin sweat

Key HPI features: 3-week-old male presenting with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, foul-smelling oily stools, and history of meconium ileus at birth where quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis Sweat Chloride test confirms elevated chloride >60 mmol/L and delta F508 CFTR mutation.

Objective/Exam findings: Obtain weight and growth trajectory, complete vital signs, hydration and respiratory assessment, and focused abdominal examination; assess for distension, tenderness, emesis, and stool output.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Treating a confirmed diagnosis as sufficient reason to overlook recurrent bowel obstruction or dehydration.
Assuming poor growth is only a feeding problem without assessing pancreatic insufficiency and caloric intake.
Starting pancreatic enzymes or vitamin supplements using an adult or unverified dose instead of a current weight-based pediatric regimen supervised by the CF team.
Attributing delayed meconium passage to cystic fibrosis alone without considering Hirschsprung disease or other neonatal obstruction when the presentation is atypical.
dangerous_errors: Missing bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal distension, peritonitis, shock, or dehydration; these require urgent emergency evaluation and pediatric surgical input when obstruction is suspected.
Delaying assessment of poor intake, weight loss, hypernatremic dehydration, or hypoglycemia in a young infant.
Giving fluids, pancreatic enzyme replacement, or fat-soluble vitamins without confirming the infant's current weight, hydration status, and specialist-directed pediatric dosing.
Discharging an infant with suspected obstruction, inadequate feeding, or unreliable follow-up before stabilization and a clear escalation plan.
management_principles: Assess immediate stability and escalate to emergency care for red flags; obtain abdominal imaging and involve pediatric surgery for possible obstruction.
Coordinate urgent follow-up with a pediatric CF center, gastroenterology, dietitian, and pulmonology as indicated.
Document weight, length, head circumference, feeding frequency and volume, wet diapers, stool pattern, and serial growth measurements.

The CF team should initiate and teach weight- and feed-based pancreatic enzyme replacement when pancreatic insufficiency is confirmed, with appropriate fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and monitoring.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Do not provide a fixed enzyme, vitamin, or fluid dose in this scenario: newborn and infant dosing must use current measured weight and local pediatric/CF protocols.
The history is provided by a parent or guardian; confirm feeding, diaper counts, medications, allergies, newborn-screen results, and access to urgent care with that caregiver.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Cystic Fibrosis Meconium Ileus and Failure to Thrive: newborn infant with failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours, abdominal distension, and salty skin sweat. 3-week-old male presenting with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, foul-smelling oily stools, and history of meconium ileus at birth where quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis Sweat Chloride test confirms elevated chloride >60 mmol/L and delta F508 CFTR mutation.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain weight, length, head circumference, temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, hydration status, urine output, and focused respiratory and abdominal examination. Assess for distension, tenderness, bilious emesis, stool output, and signs of dehydration.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Cystic Fibrosis Meconium Ileus and Failure to Thrive.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess for recurrent intestinal obstruction, dehydration, and poor weight gain; send to emergency care for bilious emesis, worsening distension, lethargy, fever, poor perfusion, or reduced urine output. Involve pediatric gastroenterology, pulmonology/CF center, nutrition, and surgery if obstruction is suspected. Begin individualized nutritional support, pancreatic enzyme replacement when exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is confirmed, and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation through the CF team using current weight-based pediatric dosing.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Cystic Fibrosis Meconium Ileus and Failure to Thrive
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for newborn infant with failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours, abdominal distension, and salty skin sweat
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for pediatrics
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.diagnosis: Cystic fibrosis with meconium ileus and failure to thrive
teaching.one_liner: 3-week-old male with history of meconium ileus at birth, now with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, and salty-tasting skin.
differentials: Hirschsprung disease or another neonatal intestinal obstruction
Sepsis or dehydration contributing to poor feeding and poor weight gain
Cow's milk protein allergy or other causes of malabsorption
red_flags: History of meconium ileus at birth
Bilious vomiting, worsening abdominal distension, fever, lethargy, poor feeding, reduced urine output, or signs of dehydration

must_ask.objective: Confirm the meconium ileus history at birth
must_ask.say: Was there any problem with him passing his first stool after birth?
Can you describe his stools — are they oily, foul-smelling, or floating?

must_ask.objective: Ask about the salty skin observation
must_ask.say: Have you noticed his skin tasting salty when you kiss him?
How has his weight gain been compared to what's expected?

must_ask.objective: Explain the confirmed diagnosis and urgent specialty referral
must_ask.say: The sweat test and genetic result support cystic fibrosis, so we need a specialized cystic fibrosis team to assess his feeding, growth, and bowel symptoms promptly.

history.answer: My three-week-old baby boy is not gaining any weight, and his diapers have been filled with large amounts of pale, greasy poop.
He weighed 3.2 kilograms at birth, but when we weighed him at the clinic yesterday, he was down to 3.0 kilograms.
He is constantly hungry and feeds eagerly every two hours, finishing a full four ounces each time without losing his appetite.
He latches well onto the bottle, swallows smoothly, and never chokes or coughs while feeding.
He spits up a tiny amount of milk after burping, but he has never had forceful or greenish vomiting.
He passes four to six very large, foul-smelling bowel movements every day, but I have never seen any blood or dark tarry stool.
His stools are bulky, pale yellow, and greasy, often leaving an oily film on his diapers and wipes.
After he was born, he did not pass his first dark meconium stool for over two days because thick plugs blocked his bowels.
Whenever I kiss his forehead or cheek, his skin tastes noticeably salty.
His belly often looks swollen and round, but it feels soft and seems a little less bloated after he has a bowel movement.
No, his hands do not shake, he does not tremble, and his heart rate seems normal to me.
He drinks his milk ravenously and wets about five or six diapers a day, which seems normal for his fluids.
No, he has not had any fever, chills, or night sweats since he came home.
He breathes comfortably through his nose and has not had any coughing, wheezing, or chest congestion.
No, I have checked all over his neck, armpits, and groin, and I have not felt any lumps or bumps.
No one in our home or extended family has ever had tuberculosis or a chronic cough.
He cries with tears and his mouth looks moist, producing around five to six wet diapers each day.

I thought maybe he has a severe milk allergy or my breast milk isn't rich enough, since his dirty diapers are greasy and he isn't putting on weight. I'm terrified that he's starving and won't develop normally because nothing he eats seems to stay in him.
I'm hoping you can prescribe a special formula or drops that his stomach can actually digest so he can gain weight.
Aside from the bowel obstruction he had right after birth, he has no other chronic illnesses or diagnoses.
He was kept in the special care nursery for four days after birth to clear the blockage with enemas, but he never needed surgery.
He is not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter remedies, or infant vitamins right now.
He has not had any allergic reactions to formulas or medications so far.
No one in our family has cystic fibrosis, childhood lung trouble, or severe digestive disorders.
He was born full-term at 39 weeks through a normal vaginal birth without any complications during labor.
He tracks objects with his eyes and kicks his legs normally, though he looks very thin compared to other newborns.
He received his initial Hepatitis B immunization at the hospital right after delivery.
He lives with my husband and me in a clean, heated apartment with plenty of family support.
Neither of us smokes, and we never allow anyone to smoke near him or in our house.
Neither parent drinks alcohol or uses any drugs.
He stays at home with me full-time, does not attend daycare, and has not been around anyone who was ill.

exam.finding: Temperature 36.8°C, heart rate 138 bpm, respiratory rate 38 breaths/min, blood pressure 74/48 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Weight is 3.0 kg, falling below the 3rd percentile from a birth weight of 3.2 kg, with notable loss of subcutaneous fat.
Alert and interactive infant with thin extremities, sunken buttocks, and mild abdominal prominence, but no acute respiratory distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are clear and non-icteric.
Oral mucous membranes are moist, lips are pink, and anterior fontanelle is flat and soft.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable.
Bilateral breath sounds are clear and symmetric without crackles, wheezes, or stridor.
Regular rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds, and no audible murmurs or gallops.
Abdomen is mildly distended with visible superficial veins, but no surgical scars, discoloration, or hernia.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants.
Abdomen is soft and mildly tympanitic without guarding, localized rigidity, or palpable masses.
Liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin with a smooth edge, and spleen is not palpable.
Skin turgor is preserved with instant recoil, and no rashes, jaundice, or ecchymoses are present.
No peripheral edema, femoral and pedal pulses are strong and equal, and capillary refill time is under two seconds.
